95	
96	Per-task DAF values reveal a bimodal structure: 5 of 11 task types are \emph{death-dominated} (DAF $\geq 0.95$: \texttt{inclined-plane}, \texttt{freeze}, \texttt{meas-melt-point}, \texttt{id-life-stages-2}, \texttt{grow-fruit}), where virtually all routing signal derives from death asymmetry, while the remaining 6 are \emph{genuine-deterministic} ($0 < \text{DAF} < 0.95$), exhibiting non-trivial non-death score differences alongside death effects. Notably, \texttt{find-non-living-thing} (DAF $= 0$) falls entirely in the latter category.
97	
98	All 129 death events across both strategies are triggered by a single action type: \texttt{focus on <location>}. This universality is task-independent. Among internal-strategy deaths, 68\% are preceded by \emph{exploration loops}---the agent cycles between locations without task progress before issuing a lethal focus action. The top lethal locations are \texttt{workshop} (21 deaths), \texttt{inventory} (15), and \texttt{kitchen} (11). The deterministic strategy avoids these loops because its constrained action space excludes invalid navigation. All deaths occur at the terminal step of their respective episodes, which is a structural property of ScienceWorld: a lethal action immediately ends the episode. When the internal strategy dies but deterministic survives (70 episodes, 28.6\% of total), the internal agent completes only 65\% as many steps (mean 19.4 vs.\ 30).
99	
100	\subsection{Ablations}
101	\label{sec:ablations}
102	
103	\paragraph{Reasoning depth.} We compare chain-of-thought reasoning (deep internal) against direct-answer generation (fast internal) on 6 overlapping task types. The two strategies are statistically indistinguishable (Mann--Whitney $p = 0.83$, $|d| \leq 0.31$) with near-identical death rates (41.8\% vs.\ 42.5\%), confirming that the 2-way routing design (deterministic vs.\ internal) is sufficient---finer-grained internal-mode distinctions do not yield additional routing signal in this setting.
104	
105	\paragraph{Router model size.} We train routers at three scales---Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-1.7B, and Qwen3-4B---using the same implicit-router architecture and a unified evaluation pipeline (\texttt{enable\_thinking=False} for all models). On a 2-seed subset (seeds 42, 43), balanced accuracy is $59.1 \pm 4.7\%$ (0.6B), $53.1 \pm 6.4\%$ (1.7B), and $58.5 \pm 5.5\%$ (4B); all differences fall within seed variance (1.7B 8-seed std $= 5.8$\,pp across the full seed set reported in \S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}). The smallest model matches or exceeds larger ones, consistent with the routing signal being dominated by a simple death-avoidance pattern that a 0.6B model can already capture---scaling the router cannot extract value from signal that does not exist.

content.content: {"result":"{\"success\": true, \"data\": {\"path\": \"/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0509_12/projects/simgate-modular-routing/paper_framing.md\", \"content\": \"# Paper Framing — simgate-modular-routing\\n\\n## Target Venue\\n- **EMNLP 2026 Main Conference — Long Paper (8 pages + references)**\\n- Deadline: ARR May 25, 2026 (10 days remaining)\\n- D050: Upgraded from short paper (4p, Findings) per user directive\\n\\n## Core Insight\\n\\nLLM agents on rule-governed environments face catastrophic failures from hallucinated state transitions. Deterministic external computation (environment simulators, code interpreters) eliminates these failures — but what exactly does routing learn? We introduce episode-level counterfactual analysis (per-step oracle labeling degenerates to 97.4% ties in sparse-reward settings) and discover that **death avoidance accounts for ~90% of routing signal** on ScienceWorld (Δ_full=+29.60 [A], Δ_nd=+2.84 [A], DAF=90.41% [A]; Pearson r=0.9698, p=8.12e-07 [A] across 11 task types / 245 episodes [A]; source: plan-012-full). Non-death performance difference is small but non-negligible (Δ_nd/Δ_full=9.6% [A]). Key exception: find-non-living-thing (n=40, zero deaths, Δ_full=+9.58, all non-death performance difference) [A]. The contribution is the empirical finding (death avoidance dominance) + the diagnostic methodology (episode-level counterfactual labeling), not the router architecture itself.\\n\\n## Core Claims (3 claims for long paper)\\n\\n**C1 (Death avoidance dominates routing signal)**: On ScienceWorld, deterministic simulation dramatically outperforms LLM reasoning (Δ_full=+29.60 [A]), with **death avoidance as the dominant mechanism** (90.41% of the performance gap [A], measured by Δ decomposition; plan-012-full, 11 tasks / 245 eps [A]). Episode-level label distribution: det-preferred 86 / internal-preferred 9 / no-preference 150 (out of 245 episodes) [A]. Death rates: internal 42.9% / deterministic 16.3% [A]. Non-death score deltas are small but non-negligible (Δ_nd=+2.84 [A], 9.6% of Δ_full [A]). Key exception: find-non-living-thing (n=40, zero deaths, Δ_full=+9.58, all non-death performance difference) [A]. Pearson r=0.9698 (p=8.12e-07) [A] between per-task death rate difference and Δ_full across 11 task types [A]. The value of deterministic computation in interactive environments is concentrated in catastrophic failure prevention, not positive task guidance.\\n\\n**C2 (Episode-level counterfactual labeling as diagnostic methodology)**: Per-step oracle labeling degenerates in sparse-reward environments (97.4% tie rate on ScienceWorld). Episode-level counterfactual analysis — running complete episodes under pure-internal and pure-deterministic strategies — overcomes this circularity and reveals the death-avoidance mechanism. The resulting labels train a lightweight router (Qwen3-1.7B) that serves as a **diagnostic probe** for LLM failure modes. [Hypothesis, pending plan-005]: the router may learn within-task-type early warning signals of catastrophic failure from early observations, beyond simple task-type classification.\\n\\n**C3 (Cross-model generality + cross-domain contrast)** [NEW for long paper]:\\n- **Cross-model mechanism verification** [Llama-3.1-8B pilot, D054→D055 corrected]: Death dominance fully replicates across model families — **both mechanism and direction consistent**. Llama pilot (freeze + find-non-living-thing, N=10): freeze's only non-tie label = death_asymmetry (internal died, det survived — same direction as Qwen where internal death rate 42.9% vs det 16.3%); find-non-living-thing has 0 deaths, all labels from score_comparison (consistent with Qwen). Llama-8B substantially weaker on ScienceWorld (most scores 0, >80% no-preference expected at scale), limiting full-scale comparison — pilot positioned as mechanism verification, not performance validation.\\n- **Cross-domain negative contrast** [MATH, clean N=300]: In environments WITHOUT catastrophic failure penalties (MATH: no death, no -100), the routing signal reverses direction — internal reasoning directionally outperforms code interpretation (+4.3pp, McNemar p=0.079). Label distribution inverts: 30 internal-preferred / 17 det-preferred (ratio 1.76:1) vs ScienceWorld's 9 / 86 (ratio 0.10:1). Dual-line evidence: (1) accuracy gap directional but not two-sided significant, (2) label distribution inversion is independent strong evidence. Cross-environment correlation (not causal — task/action/reward structure differ). Level 5 gap > Level 4 gap. One-sided bootstrap p=0.032 but not pre-registered, so paper uses conservative two-sided framing.\\n\\n**D013 note**: C1 no longer claims \\\"selective > unconditional.\\\" Router training (plan-002/003) proceeds — if router ≈ always-det, that IS the finding; comparison with rule-based baseline (plan-011) quantifies whether learned routing adds value over keyword heuristics.\\n\\n## Positioning vs Tool-Use Literature (Dream-driven addition)\\n\\n**Critical gap identified by all 3 Dream tiers**: The core pipeline (counterfactual labels → SFT small classifier → selective invocation) is standard in tool-use learning. Must position against:\\n- **Toolformer** (Schick et al. 2024): Self-supervised tool-use learning via API call insertion. SimGate differs: hindsight labels from environment forking (not self-supervised), safety-aware framing (not general tool selection).\\n- **ART** (Paranjape et al. 2023): Automated tool selection via LLM reasoning. SimGate: dedicated lightweight router, not LLM-as-router.\\n- **Chameleon** (Lu et al. 2024): LLM-as-planner routing to diverse tools. SimGate: single modality (deterministic computation), explicit small router.\\n- **ToolkenGPT** (Hao et al. 2024): Token-level tool triggers. SimGate: step-level routing with counterfactual labels.\\n\\n**Our differentiation**: (1) Episode-level counterfactual labeling — overcomes per-step oracle circularity in sparse-reward environments (97.4% tie rate), providing ground-truth episode outcomes rather than tie-break artifacts. (2) Empirical finding: death avoidance accounts for ~90% of routing signal [A] — quantifies WHERE and WHY tool invocation helps (catastrophic failure prevention, not positive guidance). (3) Diagnostic framework — counterfactual analysis + router as probe reveals systematic LLM failure modes across task categories. (4) The contribution is the finding + methodology, not the router architecture — this distinguishes from \\\"we built a better tool selector\\\" papers.\\n\\n**Paper must include a dedicated Related Work section** (not just intro paragraphs). Minimum coverage: tool-use learning (Toolformer, ART, Chameleon), adaptive computation (CogRouter, ARES, Mixture-of-Depths), world model routing (ITP-R, Dyna-Think), agent frameworks (ReAct).\\n\\n## Story Spine\\n\\n- **Problem**: LLM agents hallucinate state transitions on rule-governed environments (temperature physics, chemical reactions), leading to catastrophic failures. ITP-R routes to an approximate LLM world model but underperforms pure internal reasoning (62.58 vs CogRouter 84.6 on ScienceWorld). ReTool/AgentMath learn when to invoke code interpreters but use implicit routing entangled with the backbone. Tool-use learning methods (Toolformer, ART, Chameleon) learn general tool selection but don't specialize for catastrophic failure prevention or use counterfactual trajectory labeling.\\n\\n- **Our framing**: We use episode-level counterfactual analysis to understand WHAT routing learns. Per-step oracle labeling degenerates (97.4% tie rate on ScienceWorld), so we run complete episodes under pure-internal and pure-deterministic strategies, comparing episode-level outcomes. Key finding: ~90% of routing signal is death avoidance [A] — deterministic computation's value is almost entirely concentrated in preventing catastrophic failures (-100 penalties). Non-death performance difference is small but non-negligible (Δ_nd=+2.84, 9.6% of Δ_full [A]). A router trained on these labels becomes a diagnostic probe for LLM failure modes, but (per D013) is structurally limited to task-level risk classification under episode-level labels.\\n\\n- **Headline result template**: \\\"Episode-level counterfactual analysis across 11 ScienceWorld task types (245 episodes) [A] reveals that death avoidance accounts for 90.41% of routing signal [A] between internal LLM reasoning and deterministic computation (Δ_full=+29.60, Δ_nd=+2.84 [A]; r=0.9698, p=8.12e-07 [A]). We propose this analysis as a diagnostic methodology for understanding when and why tool invocation helps LLM agents.\\\"\\n\\n## Paper Structure (8-page long paper)\\n\\n| Section | Pages | Content |\\n|---------|-------|---------|\\n| Abstract | 0.3 | Counterfactual analysis framing, death avoidance finding (multi-model), headline numbers, cross-domain evidence |\\n| Introduction | 1.2 | Problem (LLM catastrophic failures) + gap (per-step oracle degeneracy) + contribution (methodology + finding + cross-model/domain validation) |\\n| Related Work | 1.0 | Tool-use learning (Toolformer/ART/Chameleon/ToolkenGPT), adaptive computation (CogRouter/ARES/MoD), world model routing (ITP-R/Dyna-Think), safe RL, counterfactual-in-RL (Amitai/Gajcin/Olson) |\\n| Method | 1.5 | Full formalism: counterfactual framework definition, labeling pipeline (pseudocode/algorithm), DAF derivation + properties, router architecture, death decomposition framework |\\n| Experiments | 3.0 | §4.1 ScienceWorld death decomposition (core, Qwen2.5-7B); §4.2 Multi-model validation (Model B on same tasks); §4.3 Cross-domain negative contrast: MATH 200-300 problems (internal > code interpreter → confirms death avoidance mechanism); §4.4 Temporal analysis + failure modes; §4.5 Ablations (router, labeling quality, keyword baseline structural failure) |\\n| Discussion | 0.5 | Implications for router design, scaling predictions (stronger models → lower death rate → lower DAF), when methodology applies vs doesn't |\\n| Conclusion | 0.5 | Summary + limitations + future work |\\n| References | ~1.0 | Not counted in 8-page limit |\\n\\n## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns & Mitigations\\n\\n1. **\\\"Novelty is incremental — just SFT a small model to classify\\\"**\\n   - Mitigation: Contribution is the empirical finding (death avoidance mechanism + routing patterns) more than the architecture. Router-as-diagnostic-probe reveals systematic LLM failure modes. Explicit vs implicit ablation quantifies the gap.\\n\\n2. **\\\"Only one benchmark (ScienceWorld)\\\"**\\n   - Mitigation [UPGRADED for long paper]: Multi-model validation (§4.2) shows finding holds across model families. MATH 500-problem evaluation (§4.3) demonstrates cross-domain applicability (code interpreter as deterministic oracle). ALFWorld exploratory evidence in Discussion.\\n\\n3. **\\\"Comparison unfair — CogRouter uses RL (CoPO), you use SFT\\\"**\\n   - Mitigation: Our primary comparison is SimGate vs ablated baselines (always-internal, always-deterministic, random, heuristic) — all same training budget. CogRouter/ITP-R cited from papers for context.\\n\\n4. **\\\"Death avoidance is trivial — just always use deterministic\\\"**\\n   - Mitigation: We do NOT claim selective > unconditional deterministic. Our contribution is the empirical finding that death avoidance dominates routing signal (~90% [A]), and the methodology that reveals this. Always-deterministic is a strong baseline — the interesting question is WHY (death avoidance), not WHETHER to route selectively. Plan-011 rule-based comparison + plan-012 death decomposition quantify this.\\n\\n5. **\\\"DAgger gap — SFT on pure-strategy trajectories may not transfer to mixed-strategy deployment\\\"**\\n   - Mitigation: Acknowledge explicitly (cite Ross et al. 2011). Plan C exacerbates this: router trains on always-internal/always-deterministic trajectories but deploys on mixed. Report train/test gap. If significant, discuss DAgger-style iterative relabeling as extension. Note: Plan C's episode-level labels avoid oracle circularity (no per-step tie-breaking), which is a methodological advantage even if distribution shift remains.\\n\\n6. **\\\"ScienceWorld's -100 penalty inflates gains\\\"** (Dream all 3 tiers)\\n   - Mitigation: Report gains WITH and WITHOUT death episodes separately. If non-death gains are small, honestly acknowledge that the primary value is catastrophic failure prevention — this IS our framing. Also report: what fraction of routing labels are genuine vs tie-break artifacts.\\n\\n7. **\\\"Missing tool-use literature — this is just Toolformer\\\"** (Dream all 3 tiers, CRITICAL)\\n   - Mitigation: Dedicated Related Work section. Position against Toolformer/ART/Chameleon. Differentiation: counterfactual trajectory labeling (not self-supervised), safety-aware framing (not general tool selection), explicit modular router (not LLM-as-router). (4) Episode-level counterfactual labeling — overcomes per-step oracle circularity in sparse-reward environments (97.4% tie rate).\\n\\n8. **\\\"Rule-based routing baseline missing\\\"** (Dream median + worst)\\n   - Mitigation: **D014 resolved — keyword routing structurally fails.** Two keyword lists tested: v1 (generic verbs incl. connect) → ≈always-det (85.8%); v2 (science-only: heat/boil/melt/freeze) → ≈always-internal (4.9%, near-zero hits). ScienceWorld actions use generic interaction verbs, not science keywords. Paper positions this as \\\"structural failure analysis\\\" — keyword heuristics fundamentally cannot capture routing signal in this environment, supporting the need for learned/observation-based approaches. D014: keywords v2 (science-only verbs), v1 had connect/disconnect degeneracy.\\n\\n## Venue Fit Risks (Long Paper, Main Track)\\n\\n- EMNLP LLM Agents track is a natural fit (tool use + planning + evaluation)\\n- Long paper needs: breadth (multi-model + cross-domain) + depth (temporal analysis + failure taxonomy) + methodology contribution\\n- Risk: \\\"Analysis paper, no method contribution\\\" — mitigate by positioning counterfactual labeling framework as reusable methodology, not just one-off analysis. Algorithm box + formal definitions elevate from ad hoc to principled.\\n- Risk: \\\"Death avoidance is the only signal\\\" — mitigate: multi-model validation shows it's a general phenomenon; MATH shows methodology generalizes; Discussion section addresses when/why this applies.\\n- Risk: Router ≈ always-det → novelty concern. **D014: keyword routing structurally fails on ScienceWorld** — positive finding supporting learned approaches.\\n- Risk: Scaling concern (stronger models → less death → less routing signal) — address honestly in Discussion as a feature not bug: the methodology DETECTS when routing adds value.\\n\\n## Key Differences from IDEA_BRIEF / Short Paper\\n\\n1. **D050 scope expansion**: From short paper (4p, ScienceWorld only) to long paper (8p, multi-model + cross-domain).\\n2. **C3 added**: Cross-model generality claim (pending multi-model experiment).\\n3. **MATH upgraded**: From \\\"future work\\\" to §4.3 full evaluation (500 problems).\\n4. **Structure**: Full Related Work + Discussion sections; Method expanded with formalism.\\n5. **Framing unchanged**: Core insight remains death avoidance dominance + diagnostic methodology.\\n\\n## Robustness Check (30-task prescreening, appendix only)\\n\\nA broader prescreening analysis across 30 task types / 249 episodes [B] provides robustness support: Δ_full=+38.33 [B], Δ_nd=+0.48 [B], DAF=98.75% [B], r=0.9864 [B]. The higher DAF in prescreening reflects the inclusion of many low-n task types where death dominance is even more pronounced. These numbers appear only in the appendix.\\n\\n## 数据源权威声明\\n\\n- **主表（A）**: plan-012-full, 11 tasks / 245 episodes — 所有主文引用\\n- **Robustness（B）**: prescreening, 30 tasks / 249 episodes — 仅 appendix\\n- **绝对不引用**: death_decomposition_report.json（文件名误导，实际是 30-task 数据）\\n- **绝对不引用**: results/plan_c_test_labels/implicit_sft.jsonl（标签损坏，no-preference→internal 映射错误）\\n\", \"total_chars\": 15562, \"truncated\": false}, \"error\": null, \"metadata\": {}}"}

1	\section{Introduction}
2	
3	Large language models deployed as interactive agents must repeatedly decide \emph{how} to compute: reason internally, or delegate to an external tool.
4	A Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct agent navigating ScienceWorld \cite{scienceworld-2022}---a text-based science simulation with 30 task types---faces this choice at every step. Tracking temperature thresholds, container states, and multi-step procedures via internal reasoning is error-prone: the model may hallucinate that water has boiled when the stove was never activated, or that an object has been moved when the action was invalid. Deterministic external computation (environment simulators, code interpreters) eliminates such hallucinations via exact state transitions. The practical question for agent design is therefore: \emph{when should an agent route computation externally versus reasoning internally?}
5	
6	Existing routing approaches frame this as a capability or efficiency decision.
7	Toolformer \cite{toolformer-2023} teaches models to insert API calls when doing so reduces perplexity; ART \cite{art-2023} decomposes tasks into tool-augmented programs; Chameleon \cite{chameleon-2023} selects among heterogeneous modules (search, code, vision) per subtask.
8	More recent adaptive-computation methods route to different reasoning depths \cite{cogrouter-2026,ares-2026} or model tiers \cite{mtrouter-2026}.
9	The shared assumption is that routing signal stems from diverse sources---accuracy, latency, capability matching---and that a learned router can exploit this signal to improve over any fixed strategy.
10	But this assumption has never been systematically verified: \emph{what actually drives the value of routing decisions in interactive environments?}
11	
12	We find a surprisingly concentrated answer: \textbf{death avoidance accounts for ${\sim}$90\% of the routing signal} (at default penalty $P{=}100$) in ScienceWorld.
13	The internal strategy's hallucination-induced failures trigger catastrophic agent death (a $-100$ penalty), while the deterministic strategy survives the same episodes.
14	Once death episodes are removed, the performance gap between strategies nearly vanishes.
15	
16	Reaching this conclusion requires a methodological contribution.
17	The standard approach to generating routing labels---per-step oracle comparison---degenerates under sparse rewards.
18	In ScienceWorld, non-zero reward arrives only at episode termination; 97.4\% of steps (across 11 prescreened task types) produce identical scores regardless of modality, leaving no step-level signal to learn from (\S\ref{sec:collection}).
19	Keyword-based heuristics also fail structurally, as ScienceWorld actions lack science-specific terminology (\S\ref{sec:baselines}).

\section{Introduction}

Large language models deployed as interactive agents must repeatedly decide \emph{how} to compute: reason internally, or delegate to an external tool.
A Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct agent navigating ScienceWorld \cite{scienceworld-2022}---a text-based science simulation with 30 task types---faces this choice at every step. Tracking temperature thresholds, container states, and multi-step procedures via internal reasoning is error-prone: the model may hallucinate that water has boiled when the stove was never activated, or that an object has been moved when the action was invalid. Deterministic external computation (environment simulators, code interpreters) eliminates such hallucinations via exact state transitions. The practical question for agent design is therefore: \emph{when should an agent route computation externally versus reasoning internally?}

Existing routing approaches frame this as a capability or efficiency decision.
Toolformer \cite{toolformer-2023} teaches models to insert API calls when doing so reduces perplexity; ART \cite{art-2023} decomposes tasks into tool-augmented programs; Chameleon \cite{chameleon-2023} selects among heterogeneous modules (search, code, vision) per subtask.
More recent adaptive-computation methods route to different reasoning depths \cite{cogrouter-2026,ares-2026} or model tiers \cite{mtrouter-2026}.
The shared assumption is that routing signal stems from diverse sources---accuracy, latency, capability matching---and that a learned router can exploit this signal to improve over any fixed strategy.
But this assumption has never been systematically verified: \emph{what actually drives the value of routing decisions in interactive environments?}

We find a surprisingly concentrated answer: \textbf{death avoidance accounts for ${\sim}$90\% of the routing signal} (at default penalty $P{=}100$) in ScienceWorld.
The internal strategy's hallucination-induced failures trigger catastrophic agent death (a $-100$ penalty), while the deterministic strategy survives the same episodes.
Once death episodes are removed, the performance gap between strategies nearly vanishes.

Reaching this conclusion requires a methodological contribution.
The standard approach to generating routing labels---per-step oracle comparison---degenerates under sparse rewards.
In ScienceWorld, non-zero reward arrives only at episode termination; 97.4\% of steps (across 11 prescreened task types) produce identical scores regardless of modality, leaving no step-level signal to learn from (\S\ref{sec:collection}).
Keyword-based heuristics also fail structurally, as ScienceWorld actions lack science-specific terminology (\S\ref{sec:baselines}).
We instead propose \emph{episode-level counterfactual analysis}: run complete episodes under pure-internal (ReAct \cite{react-2023}) and pure-deterministic strategies, then compare episode outcomes to generate routing labels (\S\ref{sec:collection}).

Among task types exhibiting meaningful routing signal in prescreening (11 of 30 available ScienceWorld task types, 245 episode pairs), the full deterministic advantage is $\Delta_{\text{full}} = +29.60$ points.
Excluding death episodes, the gap collapses to $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +2.84$; 78.9\% of non-tie labels (75 of 95) arise from death asymmetry---a penalty-independent measure.
The penalty-sensitive Death Avoidance Factor (DAF; \S\ref{sec:daf}) is ${\sim}90\%$ at the default penalty $P{=}100$, ranging from 50\% ($P{=}10$) to 98\% ($P{=}500$).
The per-task correlation between death-rate differential and performance gap is $r = 0.97$ ($p < 10^{-6}$, $n = 11$), confirming that death avoidance is the dominant mechanism across task types (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}).

Two cross-context checks probe the specificity of this finding.
First, a MATH Level~4--5 evaluation (300 problems), using a code interpreter as the deterministic modality, shows a marginally significant reversal ($+4.3$~pp, $p = 0.079$): internal reasoning outperforms code interpreter---the opposite direction from ScienceWorld.
In the absence of death risk, the deterministic advantage vanishes.
Second, a preliminary cross-model pilot with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ($N{=}10$ episode pairs, 2 task types) shows directionally consistent death patterns within ScienceWorld (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}), suggesting the phenomenon is not specific to a single model, though full-scale multi-model validation remains future work.
As a downstream consequence, a trained router (Qwen3-1.7B with LoRA) achieves only 57.6\% balanced accuracy (\S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Routing signal decomposition.}
    We identify step-level oracle degeneracy in sparse-reward environments and introduce episode-level counterfactual analysis with the DAF metric, a methodology for quantifying what fraction of routing signal derives from catastrophic-failure avoidance (\S\ref{sec:collection}--\ref{sec:daf}).

    \item \textbf{Death avoidance dominance.}
    On ScienceWorld, 78.9\% of non-tie routing labels stem from death asymmetry. The penalty-dependent DAF metric reaches ${\sim}90\%$ at $P{=}100$ but varies substantially across penalty settings (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}--\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).

    \item \textbf{Cross-context validation.}
    On MATH ($N{=}300$), where death risk is absent, the routing signal reverses direction (\S\ref{sec:discussion}), providing evidence that the finding is driven by failure structure rather than an inherent advantage of deterministic computation.
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows.
\S\ref{sec:method} describes the counterfactual collection procedure, episode-level labeling, and the DAF metric.
\S\ref{sec:death-decomp} presents the death avoidance decomposition and correlation analysis.
\S\ref{sec:baselines}--\ref{sec:cross-model} report baselines, router diagnostics, and cross-model verification.
\S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses cross-environment evidence and implications.

1	\section{Experiments}
2	
3	\subsection{Death Avoidance Decomposition}
4	\label{sec:death-decomp}
5	
6	\begin{figure}[t]
7	\centering
8	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig1_daf_scatter.pdf}
9	\caption{Per-task scatter plot: death rate differential (internal minus deterministic) vs.\ performance gap ($\Delta_{\text{full}}$). Pearson $r = 0.9698$ ($p = 8.12 \times 10^{-7}$). Each point is one of 11 ScienceWorld task types.}
10	\label{fig:decomposition}
11	\end{figure}
12	
13	The full performance gap between deterministic and internal strategies across 245 episodes is $\Delta_{\text{full}} = +29.60$ points. When we exclude all episodes where either strategy results in agent death, the gap collapses to $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +2.84$. The resulting Death Avoidance Factor (\S\ref{sec:daf}) is ${\sim}90\%$ (at the default penalty $P{=}100$): approximately nine-tenths of the deterministic strategy's advantage over internal reasoning is attributable to death avoidance rather than superior task performance when both agents survive.
14	
15	This concentration is consistent across task types (Appendix~\ref{app:per-task}). The Pearson correlation between per-task death rate differential and $\Delta_{\text{full}}$ is $r = 0.9698$ ($p = 8.12 \times 10^{-7}$; bootstrap 95\% CI $[0.952, 0.995]$), as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:decomposition}. Spearman rank correlation is $\rho = 0.986$ ($p = 2.4 \times 10^{-8}$), and leave-one-out analysis shows $r \in [0.963, 0.980]$---no single task type is a leverage point (Appendix~\ref{app:correlation}). We note that death rate differential and $\Delta_{\text{full}}$ are structurally coupled through the penalty term $P$, so high correlation is expected when death dominates. The empirically non-trivial finding is that 78.9\% of non-tie routing labels (75 of 95) are driven by death asymmetry independent of $P$. Knowing how much more frequently the internal strategy dies is nearly sufficient to predict the full performance gap for a given task type. The internal strategy dies in 42.9\% of episodes compared to 16.3\% for deterministic computation---a 2.6$\times$ ratio that drives the bulk of the observed score difference.
16	
17	The episode-level label distribution reflects this asymmetry: of 245 episodes, 86 are \texttt{det\_preferred}, only 9 \texttt{internal\_preferred}, and 150 \texttt{no\_preference}---when internal reasoning does not cause death, it performs comparably to deterministic computation.
18	
19	Notably, the per-task DAF distribution is bimodal: \texttt{find-non-living-thing} exhibits DAF $\approx 0\%$ (routing signal entirely from non-death score differences, $\Delta = +9.58$), while all other task types exceed 85\%.
20	
21	One task reveals the residual non-death signal. \texttt{find-non-living-thing} ($n=40$) has zero deaths under both strategies yet shows $\Delta_{\text{full}} = +9.58$, entirely from non-death performance differences---deterministic computation can provide advantages through more accurate state tracking even when agents survive. However, among the 10 death-prone task types, death avoidance overwhelms non-death differences. When both modalities survive, the gap is small but non-negligible ($\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +2.84$, 9.6\% of $\Delta_{\text{full}}$).
22	
23	\subsection{Baselines}
24	\label{sec:baselines}
25	
26	\begin{table}[t]
27	\centering
28	\small
29	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
30	\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
31	\toprule
32	Strategy & Score & 95\% CI & Death \% \\
33	\midrule
34	Always-Internal & $-39.07$ & [$-46.40$, $-32.27$] & 42.9 \\
35	Always-Deterministic & $-9.47$ & [$-14.71$, $-4.29$] & 16.3 \\
36	Random & $-22.38$ & [$-28.67$, $-15.75$] & 27.8 \\
37	Oracle & $-6.58$ & [$-11.54$, $-1.70$] & 14.3 \\
38	\midrule
39	Trained Router$^\dagger$ & $-10.70$ & [$-16.33$, $-5.27$] & 17.6 \\
40	\bottomrule
41	\end{tabular}}
42	\caption{Episode-weighted mean scores on ScienceWorld (11 task types, 245 episodes). 95\% Bootstrap CIs. The oracle selects the higher-scoring strategy per episode; 96.3\% of its decisions match the always-deterministic strategy. $\dagger$\,Single seed (seed 42); balanced accuracy across 4 seeds reported in \S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}.}
43	\label{tab:baselines}
44	\end{table}
45	
46	Table~\ref{tab:baselines} reports episode-weighted mean scores and death rates for four unconditional strategies. Always-deterministic ($-9.47$) outperforms always-internal ($-39.07$) by 29.60 points, consistent with $\Delta_{\text{full}}$. The oracle, which selects the higher-scoring strategy per episode, improves only modestly to $-6.58$, with 96.3\% of its routing decisions matching always-deterministic. This \emph{oracle degeneracy} indicates that the optimal episode-level routing policy closely resembles unconditional deterministic computation---the routing signal is insufficient to improve upon simply always choosing the deterministic strategy. Random routing ($-22.38$) falls between the two pure strategies, with a death rate (27.8\%) proportional to its 50/50 allocation.
47	
48	Keyword-based routing fails structurally: match rates cluster at extremes (85.8\% or $<$5\%), precluding meaningful routing discrimination.
49	
50	\subsection{Router Training as Diagnostic}
51	\label{sec:router-diagnostic}
52	
53	A natural question is whether the episode-level counterfactual labels can train a step-level router. We investigate this as a diagnostic probe of label informativeness rather than a routing system proposal, testing two architectures.
54	
55	\paragraph{Classification head.} A linear head on LLM hidden representations, trained on episode-level labels, degenerates to always-deterministic (0\% internal recall) across all configurations (class weighting, focal loss, undersampling, temperature scaling).
56	
57	\paragraph{Implicit router.} We fine-tune Qwen3-1.7B to internalize routing decisions within its generation (Appendix~\ref{app:router-details}). Across four training seeds with a fixed data split, balanced accuracy is $57.6 \pm 0.5\%$; when the train/validation split is also varied, cross-split variance is substantially higher ($54.1 \pm 5.8\%$ across 8 seeds; Appendix~\ref{app:seed-robustness}), as the small validation set (14 episodes) amplifies split sensitivity. Both estimates are above chance but insufficient for practical routing.
58	
59	\paragraph{End-to-end evaluation.} Deployed as an episode-level router (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}), the trained router scores $-10.70$ (95\% CI $[-16.33, -5.27]$), not statistically outperforming always-deterministic ($-9.47$, $[-14.71, -4.29]$; overlapping CIs). The episode-to-step granularity mismatch is the bottleneck: when DAF $\approx 90\%$, router headroom is limited to the ${\sim}10\%$ non-death signal.
60	
61	\paragraph{Data split.} Of 245 episodes, 95 non-tie labels are split 85/15 (81 train, 14 validation; 1734/306 steps). Baselines in Table~\ref{tab:baselines} report trajectory statistics; the router score ($-10.70$) comes from fresh environment interaction.
62	
63	\paragraph{Labeling quality.} We verify label quality in Appendix~\ref{app:labeling}.
64	
65	\subsection{Cross-Model Verification}
66	\label{sec:cross-model}
67	
68	To test whether the death avoidance pattern is model-specific, we run a mechanism verification pilot with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on two task types (\texttt{freeze} and \texttt{find-non-living-thing}, 5 episode pairs each, $N{=}10$). Llama-8B achieves lower absolute ScienceWorld scores than Qwen-2.5-7B, reflecting weaker task-level capability, but the death pattern direction is consistent across model families.
69	
70	On \texttt{freeze}, the internal strategy dies in 40\% of episodes versus 20\% for deterministic (Qwen: 55\%/25\%)---the same directional asymmetry. The single non-tie episode arises from death asymmetry: the internal strategy dies while deterministic survives, producing a det-preferred label consistent with the Qwen pattern. On \texttt{find-non-living-thing}, both strategies achieve 0\% death rate under Llama, matching Qwen exactly; the 3 det-preferred labels arise from non-death score differences.
71	
72	\begin{table}[t]
73	\centering
74	\small
75	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
76	\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccc@{}}
77	\toprule
78	Task & Model & D\%\textsubscript{int} & D\%\textsubscript{det} & $\Delta$D\% & D / I / N \\
79	\midrule
80	freeze & Qwen-7B & 55 & 25 & +30 & 6 / 0 / 14 \\
81	freeze & Llama-8B & 40 & 20 & +20 & 1 / 0 / 4 \\
82	\midrule
83	find-non-living & Qwen-7B & 0 & 0 & 0 & 16 / 4 / 20 \\
84	find-non-living & Llama-8B & 0 & 0 & 0 & 3 / 1 / 1 \\
85	\bottomrule
86	\end{tabular}}
87	\caption{Cross-model death rate comparison. Llama pilot: $n{=}5$ episodes per task; Qwen: from Table~\ref{tab:per-task}. $\Delta$D\%: internal minus deterministic death rate. D/I/N: det-preferred / internal-preferred / no-preference labels.}
88	\label{tab:cross-model}
89	\end{table}
90	
91	Table~\ref{tab:cross-model} summarizes the comparison. This pilot ($N{=}10$ episode pairs) provides preliminary directional evidence only: the sample size precludes statistical claims. Nevertheless, observing the same death asymmetry direction in a different model family (Llama vs.\ Qwen) suggests that the pattern reflects a structural property of internal reasoning in interactive environments rather than a model-specific artifact.
92	
93	\subsection{Failure Mode Analysis}
94	\label{sec:failure-modes}
95	
96	Per-task DAF values reveal a bimodal structure: 5 of 11 task types are \emph{death-dominated} (DAF $\geq 0.95$: \texttt{inclined-plane}, \texttt{freeze}, \texttt{meas-melt-point}, \texttt{id-life-stages-2}, \texttt{grow-fruit}), where virtually all routing signal derives from death asymmetry, while the remaining 6 are \emph{genuine-deterministic} ($0 < \text{DAF} < 0.95$), exhibiting non-trivial non-death score differences alongside death effects. Notably, \texttt{find-non-living-thing} (DAF $= 0$) falls entirely in the latter category.
97	
98	All 129 death events across both strategies are triggered by a single action type: \texttt{focus on <location>}. This universality is task-independent. Among internal-strategy deaths, 68\% are preceded by \emph{exploration loops}---the agent cycles between locations without task progress before issuing a lethal focus action. The top lethal locations are \texttt{workshop} (21 deaths), \texttt{inventory} (15), and \texttt{kitchen} (11). The deterministic strategy avoids these loops because its constrained action space excludes invalid navigation. All deaths occur at the terminal step of their respective episodes, which is a structural property of ScienceWorld: a lethal action immediately ends the episode. When the internal strategy dies but deterministic survives (70 episodes, 28.6\% of total), the internal agent completes only 65\% as many steps (mean 19.4 vs.\ 30).
99	
100	\subsection{Ablations}
101	\label{sec:ablations}
102	
103	\paragraph{Reasoning depth.} We compare chain-of-thought reasoning (deep internal) against direct-answer generation (fast internal) on 6 overlapping task types. The two strategies are statistically indistinguishable (Mann--Whitney $p = 0.83$, $|d| \leq 0.31$) with near-identical death rates (41.8\% vs.\ 42.5\%), confirming that the 2-way routing design (deterministic vs.\ internal) is sufficient---finer-grained internal-mode distinctions do not yield additional routing signal in this setting.
104	
105	\paragraph{Router model size.} To test whether router capacity matters, we compare Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-4B using the same implicit-router architecture and identical training and evaluation pipelines (\texttt{enable\_thinking=False}). On a 2-seed subset (seeds 42, 43), both achieve comparable balanced accuracy ($59.1 \pm 4.7\%$ vs.\ $58.5 \pm 5.5\%$), well within seed variance (the 1.7B model's 8-seed std $= 5.8$\,pp; \S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}). A 0.6B router captures the available signal---scaling to 4B provides no benefit, consistent with the routing signal being dominated by a simple death-avoidance pattern.

1	\section{Conclusion}
2	
3	We introduced episode-level counterfactual analysis as a methodology for decomposing the routing signal in modular LLM agents into death-avoidance and non-death components. Applied to 245 ScienceWorld episodes among task types exhibiting meaningful routing signal in prescreening (11 of 30 available task types) with a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbone, this analysis reveals that 78.9\% of non-tie routing labels (75 of 95) arise from death asymmetry---a penalty-independent metric. The penalty-sensitive DAF reaches ${\sim}90\%$ at the default $P{=}100$ ($\Delta_\text{full} = 29.60$ vs.\ $\Delta_\text{nd} = 2.84$), with strong cross-task correlation ($r = 0.97$, $p < 10^{-6}$).
4	
5	Two lines of evidence support the generality of this finding. First, cross-environment analysis on MATH ($N{=}300$), where no death penalty exists, shows that the routing signal vanishes and directionally reverses: internal reasoning directionally outperforms code execution by $+4.3$ percentage points (marginally significant, $p = 0.079$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}), and the label distribution inverts from 86:9 deterministic-preferred in ScienceWorld to 30:17 internal-preferred. This contrast confirms that death avoidance, not an inherent advantage of deterministic computation, is the primary driver. Second, a Llama-3.1-8B pilot ($N{=}10$, insufficient for statistical inference) replicates the direction of the death differential, providing directional but not conclusive evidence of cross-model consistency.
6	
7	As a downstream consequence, a trained routing classifier achieves only 57.6\% balanced accuracy (54.1$\pm$5.8\% across 8 seeds)---an illustrative negative result reinforcing the death-dominance finding: the extreme class imbalance induced by death asymmetry (86:9 det:int labels) structurally constrains any classifier trained on episode-level labels (\S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).
8	
9	These results carry a practical implication: in environments with catastrophic failure modes, routing value is dominated by safety rather than efficiency. The router functions primarily as a safety critic---steering away from fatal actions---rather than as an optimizer selecting the more efficient strategy. System designers may therefore benefit from treating routing as a risk-management mechanism in such settings.
10	
11	Several directions remain open. Step-level counterfactual labeling could localize where within an episode routing decisions matter most. Stronger backbone models with lower intrinsic death rates may yield lower DAF values, revealing whether non-death routing signal emerges as the safety floor rises. Finally, environments with graded failure costs (rather than binary death) would test whether the dominance of catastrophic-failure avoidance extends to softer penalty structures.

\section{Conclusion}

The router functions primarily as a safety critic---steering away from fatal actions---rather than as an optimizer selecting the more efficient strategy. 1	\section{Related Work}
2	
3	\paragraph{Tool Use and External Computation in LLMs.}
4	A growing body of work augments language models with external tools \citep{tool-learning-survey-2024}.
5	Toolformer \cite{toolformer-2023} teaches LLMs to insert API calls via self-supervised loss filtering, while ToolkenGPT \cite{toolkengpt-2023} represents tools as special tokens in the embedding space, enabling frozen models to invoke massive tool libraries.
6	ART \cite{art-2023} decomposes tasks into multi-step programs that interleave reasoning with tool calls, and Chameleon \cite{chameleon-2023} composes heterogeneous modules (search, code, vision) via LLM-generated programs.
7	ReTool \cite{retool-2025} applies reinforcement learning to let models discover when code execution is preferable to chain-of-thought.
8	These approaches focus on \emph{learning to use tools}; our work instead asks a prior question: \emph{what signal drives the decision to route to an external modality at all?}
9	
10	Recent concurrent studies sharpen this question from multiple angles.
11	\citet{tool-overuse-illusion-2026} identify a cognitive-illusion effect in which LLMs default to external tools even when internal knowledge suffices.
12	\citet{when2tool-2026} show that tool-call decisions are already encoded in hidden states before explicit reasoning occurs.
13	\citet{tool-use-tax-2026} quantify a ``tool-use tax''---cases where invoking a tool degrades rather than improves performance.
14	\citet{to-call-or-not-2026} propose a necessity--utility--affordability framework for deciding whether to call a tool.
15	Our counterfactual decomposition provides complementary, environment-grounded evidence: in ScienceWorld, ${\sim}90\%$ of the routing signal at $P{=}100$ traces to catastrophic-failure prevention rather than general utility, offering a concrete quantification that these frameworks currently lack.
16	
17	\paragraph{Adaptive Computation and Routing.}
18	Rather than adding new tools, a parallel line of research routes inputs to different computation budgets or models.
19	CogRouter \cite{cogrouter-2026} adapts reasoning depth per step, ARES \cite{ares-2026} selects among reasoning effort levels for LLM agents, and Mixture-of-Recursions \cite{mixture-of-recursions-2025} learns token-level recursion depths within a single model.
20	MTRouter \cite{mtrouter-2026} addresses multi-turn routing across heterogeneous models by jointly embedding conversation history and model capabilities.
21	In the LLM serving setting, RouteLLM \citep{routellm-2024} learns routers from human preference data to dynamically select between strong and weak models, reducing cost without sacrificing quality.
22	These systems optimize \emph{how} to route; we focus on \emph{why} routing helps.
23	Our counterfactual analysis reveals that, in interactive environments, the dominant routing signal is not efficiency or capability matching but catastrophic-failure avoidance---a finding that could inform the objective design of future routers.
24	
25	\paragraph{Counterfactual Evaluation in RL.}
26	Counterfactual reasoning has been used to explain RL agent behavior post hoc.
27	\citet{olson2021counterfactual} generate counterfactual states via deep generative models to highlight features critical to an agent's decisions.
28	\citet{gajcin2023counterfactual} produce counterfactual action explanations that show users which alternative actions would have led to different outcomes.
29	\citet{amitai2024explaining} extend this to action-outcome explanations, contrasting observed and hypothetical trajectories at the step level.
30	A common thread is that these methods perturb \emph{individual actions} within a fixed policy to attribute credit.
31	Our approach differs in both purpose and granularity: we execute two \emph{complete episodes} under different routing strategies (LLM-only vs.\ LLM+simulator), producing prospective paired comparisons that isolate the routing signal \emph{before} any router is trained.
32	This episode-level design sidesteps compounding perturbation artifacts and directly measures the aggregate effect of modality access on task outcomes.
33	
34	\paragraph{Safe RL and Catastrophic Failure.}
35	\citet{garcia2015comprehensive} survey safe RL methods that constrain policies to avoid catastrophic outcomes, categorizing approaches into constrained optimization, risk-sensitive criteria, and external-knowledge incorporation.
36	More recent work develops principled constrained optimization methods with formal convergence guarantees for safe policy learning \citep{crpo-2021}.
37	A common mechanism is reward shaping with large negative penalties for unsafe states, which implicitly teaches agents to avoid irreversible failures.
38	Our findings connect to this literature from an analytical rather than algorithmic perspective: the counterfactual decomposition reveals that death avoidance---preventing irreversible task failure---is the dominant component of the routing signal in ScienceWorld.
39	This suggests that modality routing in interactive environments functions primarily as a safety mechanism, and that router design may benefit from explicitly modeling catastrophic-failure risk rather than treating routing as a generic capability-matching problem.
40	
41	\paragraph{LLM Agents in Interactive Environments.}
42	ScienceWorld \cite{scienceworld-2022} provides a text-based science-experiment environment requiring multi-step causal reasoning, serving as our primary testbed.
43	ALFWorld \cite{alfworld-2021} offers a complementary text-based household environment; Voyager \cite{voyager-2023} demonstrates open-ended exploration in Minecraft using LLM-driven curriculum and skill libraries.
44	ReAct \cite{react-2023} interleaves reasoning traces with environment actions and serves as our internal-reasoning baseline; Reflexion \cite{reflexion-2023} extends this with verbal self-correction across trials.
45	Reflexion \citep{reflexion-2023} extends this paradigm by augmenting agents with verbal self-reflection, maintaining an episodic memory of past failures to improve subsequent trials.
46	More recent work augments agents with world models: ITP \cite{itp-2026} uses learned world models for lookahead planning, while Dyna-Think \cite{dynathink-2025} synergizes reasoning, acting, and world-model simulation.
47	Both inherit the hallucination risks of approximate world models.
48	Our deterministic simulator modality provides exact state transitions, and our analysis shows that this exactness matters almost exclusively for death avoidance---the cases where hallucinated transitions would be most costly.

\section{Related Work}

\paragraph{Tool Use and External Computation in LLMs.}
A growing body of work augments language models with external tools \citep{tool-learning-survey-2024}.
Toolformer \cite{toolformer-2023} teaches LLMs to insert API calls via self-supervised loss filtering, while ToolkenGPT \cite{toolkengpt-2023} represents tools as special tokens in the embedding space, enabling frozen models to invoke massive tool libraries.
ART \cite{art-2023} decomposes tasks into multi-step programs that interleave reasoning with tool calls, and Chameleon \cite{chameleon-2023} composes heterogeneous modules (search, code, vision) via LLM-generated programs.
ReTool \cite{retool-2025} applies reinforcement learning to let models discover when code execution is preferable to chain-of-thought.
These approaches focus on \emph{learning to use tools}; our work instead asks a prior question: \emph{what signal drives the decision to route to an external modality at all?}

Recent concurrent studies sharpen this question from multiple angles.
\citet{tool-overuse-illusion-2026} identify a cognitive-illusion effect in which LLMs default to external tools even when internal knowledge suffices.
\citet{when2tool-2026} show that tool-call decisions are already encoded in hidden states before explicit reasoning occurs.
\citet{tool-use-tax-2026} quantify a ``tool-use tax''---cases where invoking a tool degrades rather than improves performance.
\citet{to-call-or-not-2026} propose a necessity--utility--affordability framework for deciding whether to call a tool.
Our counterfactual decomposition provides complementary, environment-grounded evidence: in ScienceWorld, ${\sim}90\%$ of the routing signal at $P{=}100$ traces to catastrophic-failure prevention rather than general utility, offering a concrete quantification that these frameworks currently lack.

\paragraph{Adaptive Computation and Routing.}
Rather than adding new tools, a parallel line of research routes inputs to different computation budgets or models.
CogRouter \cite{cogrouter-2026} adapts reasoning depth per step, ARES \cite{ares-2026} selects among reasoning effort levels for LLM agents, and Mixture-of-Recursions \cite{mixture-of-recursions-2025} learns token-level recursion depths within a single model.
MTRouter \cite{mtrouter-2026} addresses multi-turn routing across heterogeneous models by jointly embedding conversation history and model capabilities.
In the LLM serving setting, RouteLLM \citep{routellm-2024} learns routers from human preference data to dynamically select between strong and weak models, reducing cost without sacrificing quality.
These systems optimize \emph{how} to route; we focus on \emph{why} routing helps.
Our counterfactual analysis reveals that, in interactive environments, the dominant routing signal is not efficiency or capability matching but catastrophic-failure avoidance---a finding that could inform the objective design of future routers.

\paragraph{Counterfactual Evaluation in RL.}
Counterfactual reasoning has been used to explain RL agent behavior post hoc.
\citet{olson2021counterfactual} generate counterfactual states via deep generative models to highlight features critical to an agent's decisions.
\citet{gajcin2023counterfactual} produce counterfactual action explanations that show users which alternative actions would have led to different outcomes.
\citet{amitai2024explaining} extend this to action-outcome explanations, contrasting observed and hypothetical trajectories at the step level.
A common thread is that these methods perturb \emph{individual actions} within a fixed policy to attribute credit.
Our approach differs in both purpose and granularity: we execute two \emph{complete episodes} under different routing strategies (LLM-only vs.\ LLM+simulator), producing prospective paired comparisons that isolate the routing signal \emph{before} any router is trained.
This episode-level design sidesteps compounding perturbation artifacts and directly measures the aggregate effect of modality access on task outcomes.

\paragraph{Safe RL and Catastrophic Failure.}
\citet{garcia2015comprehensive} survey safe RL methods that constrain policies to avoid catastrophic outcomes, categorizing approaches into constrained optimization, risk-sensitive criteria, and external-knowledge incorporation.
More recent work develops principled constrained optimization methods with formal convergence guarantees for safe policy learning \citep{crpo-2021}.
A common mechanism is reward shaping with large negative penalties for unsafe states, which implicitly teaches agents to avoid irreversible failures.
Our findings connect to this literature from an analytical rather than algorithmic perspective: the counterfactual decomposition reveals that death avoidance---preventing irreversible task failure---is the dominant component of the routing signal in ScienceWorld.
This suggests that modality routing in interactive environments functions primarily as a safety mechanism, and that router design may benefit from explicitly modeling catastrophic-failure risk rather than treating routing as a generic capability-matching problem.

\paragraph{LLM Agents in Interactive Environments.}
ScienceWorld \cite{scienceworld-2022} provides a text-based science-experiment environment requiring multi-step causal reasoning, serving as our primary testbed.
ALFWorld \cite{alfworld-2021} offers a complementary text-based household environment; Voyager \cite{voyager-2023} demonstrates open-ended exploration in Minecraft using LLM-driven curriculum and skill libraries.
ReAct \cite{react-2023} interleaves reasoning traces with environment actions and serves as our internal-reasoning baseline; Reflexion \cite{reflexion-2023} extends this with verbal self-correction across trials.
Reflexion \citep{reflexion-2023} extends this paradigm by augmenting agents with verbal self-reflection, maintaining an episodic memory of past failures to improve subsequent trials.
More recent work augments agents with world models: ITP \cite{itp-2026} uses learned world models for lookahead planning, while Dyna-Think \cite{dynathink-2025} synergizes reasoning, acting, and world-model simulation.
Both inherit the hallucination risks of approximate world models.
Our deterministic simulator modality provides exact state transitions, and our analysis shows that this exactness matters almost exclusively for death avoidance---the cases where hallucinated transitions would be most costly.

\section{Related Work}

\paragraph{Tool Use and External Computation in LLMs.}
A growing body of work augments language models with external tools \citep{tool-learning-survey-2024}.
Toolformer \cite{toolformer-2023} teaches LLMs to insert API calls via self-supervised loss filtering, while ToolkenGPT \cite{toolkengpt-2023} represents tools as special tokens in the embedding space, enabling frozen models to invoke massive tool libraries.
ART \cite{art-2023} decomposes tasks into multi-step programs that interleave reasoning with tool calls, and Chameleon \cite{chameleon-2023} composes heterogeneous modules (search, code, vision) via LLM-generated programs.
ReTool \cite{retool-2025} applies reinforcement learning to let models discover when code execution is preferable to chain-of-thought.
These approaches focus on \emph{learning to use tools}; our work instead asks a prior question: \emph{what signal drives the decision to route to an external modality at all?}

Recent concurrent studies sharpen this question from multiple angles.
\citet{tool-overuse-illusion-2026} identify a cognitive-illusion effect in which LLMs default to external tools even when internal knowledge suffices.
\citet{when2tool-2026} show that tool-call decisions are already encoded in hidden states before explicit reasoning occurs.
\citet{tool-use-tax-2026} quantify a ``tool-use tax''---cases where invoking a tool degrades rather than improves performance.
\citet{to-call-or-not-2026} propose a necessity--utility--affordability framework for deciding whether to call a tool.
Our counterfactual decomposition provides complementary, environment-grounded evidence: in ScienceWorld, ${\sim}90\%$ of the routing signal at $P{=}100$ traces to catastrophic-failure prevention rather than general utility, offering a concrete quantification that these frameworks currently lack.

\paragraph{Adaptive Computation and Routing.}
Rather than adding new tools, a parallel line of research routes inputs to different computation budgets or models.
CogRouter \cite{cogrouter-2026} adapts reasoning depth per step, ARES \cite{ares-2026} selects among reasoning effort levels for LLM agents, and Mixture-of-Recursions \cite{mixture-of-recursions-2025} learns token-level recursion depths within a single model.
MTRouter \cite{mtrouter-2026} addresses multi-turn routing across heterogeneous models by jointly embedding conversation history and model capabilities.
In the LLM serving setting, RouteLLM \citep{routellm-2024} learns routers from human preference data to dynamically select between strong and weak models, reducing cost without sacrificing quality.
These systems optimize \emph{how} to route; we focus on \emph{why} routing helps.
Our counterfactual analysis reveals that, in interactive environments, the dominant routing signal is not efficiency or capability matching but catastrophic-failure avoidance---a finding that could inform the objective design of future routers.

\paragraph{Counterfactual Evaluation in RL.}
Counterfactual reasoning has been used to explain RL agent behavior post hoc.
\citet{olson2021counterfactual} generate counterfactual states via deep generative models to highlight features critical to an agent's decisions.
\citet{gajcin2023counterfactual} produce counterfactual action explanations that show users which alternative actions would have led to different outcomes.
\citet{amitai2024explaining} extend this to action-outcome explanations, contrasting observed and hypothetical trajectories at the step level.
A common thread is that these methods perturb \emph{individual actions} within a fixed policy to attribute credit.
Our approach differs in both purpose and granularity: we execute two \emph{complete episodes} under different routing strategies (LLM-only vs.\ LLM+simulator), producing prospective paired comparisons that isolate the routing signal \emph{before} any router is trained.
This episode-level design sidesteps compounding perturbation artifacts and directly measures the aggregate effect of modality access on task outcomes.

\paragraph{Safe RL and Catastrophic Failure.}
\citet{garcia2015comprehensive} survey safe RL methods that constrain policies to avoid catastrophic outcomes, categorizing approaches into constrained optimization, risk-sensitive criteria, and external-knowledge incorporation.
More recent work develops principled constrained optimization methods with formal convergence guarantees for safe policy learning \citep{crpo-2021}.
A common mechanism is reward shaping with large negative penalties for unsafe states, which implicitly teaches agents to avoid irreversible failures.
Our findings connect to this literature from an analytical rather than algorithmic perspective: the counterfactual decomposition reveals that death avoidance---preventing irreversible task failure---is the dominant component of the routing signal in ScienceWorld.
This suggests that modality routing in interactive environments functions primarily as a safety mechanism, and that router design may benefit from explicitly modeling catastrophic-failure risk rather than treating routing as a generic capability-matching problem.

\paragraph{LLM Agents in Interactive Environments.}
ScienceWorld \cite{scienceworld-2022} provides a text-based science-experiment environment requiring multi-step causal reasoning, serving as our primary testbed.
ALFWorld \cite{alfworld-2021} offers a complementary text-based household environment; Voyager \cite{voyager-2023} demonstrates open-ended exploration in Minecraft using LLM-driven curriculum and skill libraries.
ReAct \cite{react-2023} interleaves reasoning traces with environment actions and serves as our internal-reasoning baseline; Reflexion \cite{reflexion-2023} extends this with verbal self-correction across trials.
Reflexion \citep{reflexion-2023} extends this paradigm by augmenting agents with verbal self-reflection, maintaining an episodic memory of past failures to improve subsequent trials.
More recent work augments agents with world models: ITP \cite{itp-2026} uses learned world models for lookahead planning, while Dyna-Think \cite{dynathink-2025} synergizes reasoning, acting, and world-model simulation.
Both inherit the hallucination risks of approximate world models.
Our deterministic simulator modality provides exact state transitions, and our analysis shows that this exactness matters almost exclusively for death avoidance---the cases where hallucinated transitions would be most costly.
